title: Climate Sensitivity
objective: After this level you can explain how much warming scientists expect from doubling carbon dioxide and why the range is uncertain.
summary: Doubling CO2 would eventually warm Earth by about 3 °C, likely 2.5 to 4 °C (IPCC AR6). Clouds are the main reason the answer is still a range.

cards.headline: Double the carbon dioxide in the air. How much warmer does Earth end up?
cards.body: It may be the most important question in climate science, and the answer isn't a single number. It's a range, and the story is why.

cards.headline: One question, one name
cards.body: Scientists call it equilibrium climate sensitivity: the warming Earth eventually settles at after the carbon dioxide in the air doubles and the climate adjusts. Level 81 gave the starting point: 280 ppm or less before the Industrial Revolution. The answer counts everything that responds along the way, including the snow and water vapor feedbacks from Level 85.

cards.fact: IPCC's best estimate: doubling carbon dioxide eventually warms Earth about 3 °C, likely 2.5 to 4 °C.
cards.context: In IPCC language, likely means a 66 to 100% chance. The very likely range is 2 to 5 °C. The 2021 report narrowed the old likely range of 1.5 to 4.5 °C by combining several lines of evidence: how climate works, the measured record, past climates and models.

cards.headline: Why clouds keep it a range
cards.body: The biggest remaining uncertainty is clouds: how their amount and type will shift as the world warms. That's why sensitivity is still a range rather than one number. But the IPCC now judges it very unlikely that clouds will turn out to damp the warming, and its very likely range starts at 2 °C, not near zero.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest remaining source of uncertainty in climate sensitivity?

options.label: How much CO2 the air held in 1958
options.rationale: That was measured at Mauna Loa.

options.label: Whether CO2 traps heat at all

questions.explanation: Clouds are the largest part of the uncertainty in climate feedbacks, which keeps sensitivity a range.

questions.prompt: A new study estimates climate sensitivity at 6 °C. How does that compare with the IPCC's assessment?

options.label: It sits inside the likely range
It is above even the very likely range
It is ruled out as impossible
options.rationale: Outside the range means unlikely, not impossible.

questions.explanation: The very likely range is 2 to 5 °C, so 6 °C is judged unlikely, though not impossible.

questions.prompt: Sensitivity counts how snow, water vapor and clouds respond, not just the extra CO2. Which idea from Level 1 explains why?

options.label: Rocks and minerals never change
options.rationale: Level 1 is about links between the spheres.

options.label: Only the atmosphere affects climate
options.rationale: Level 1 showed rock reaching the sky and changing climate.

options.label: Earth's spheres are linked, so changes spread
Each sphere changes on its own schedule
options.rationale: Level 1 stressed that they affect each other.

questions.explanation: A change in the air reaches water, ice and life, so the eventual warming includes their responses.
